justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, anchored around a current level of roughly 67.7. At the one-day horizon, the estimate stays close to the current observed value because intraday and overnight moves in most financial or economic series tend to be small relative to the prevailing level, and absent any imminent scheduled catalyst, mean-reversion forces dominate. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 67.9, reflecting a mild positive trend assumption and the possibility that any near-term momentum carries forward modestly. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises to 68.5, incorporating a continuation of whatever underlying trend was present in recent data while acknowledging that a month is long enough for a meaningful directional drift to accumulate.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 3 units, consistent with typical short-run volatility. At one week, it widens to roughly 5.8 units on each side, capturing the compounding of daily fluctuations and the possibility of a moderate shock. At one month, the interval spans 13 units, acknowledging that over four weeks, macroeconomic data releases, policy decisions, or sentiment shifts could meaningfully alter the trajectory. The asymmetry in uncertainty is kept roughly symmetric here because I had no strong prior reason to expect skewed tail risks in either direction.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden policy announcements, geopolitical shocks, or unexpected data prints that arrive between now and the forecast horizon. At the one-month horizon in particular, a central bank decision, a significant earnings surprise, or an abrupt shift in market risk appetite could easily produce a move of 10 or more units, which would breach the stated interval. On the downside, a deterioration in macroeconomic sentiment or a liquidity event could drag the series well below 62. These tail scenarios were deliberately kept outside the 90% interval precisely because they are low-probability but non-negligible, and the interval is not intended to capture every conceivable outcome.

It is also worth noting that the quality of this forecast depends heavily on the stationarity and recent behavior of the underlying series, neither of which I can verify with certainty.
